subtitle: Call for papers to a pioneering symposium on network optimization and software.

tldr.problem: The early network community needed a forum to share protocol designs and file transfer techniques that were already being developed.
tldr.mechanism: Vint Cerf and colleagues issued a call for papers to the Second Symposium on Problems in the Optimization of Data Communication Systems, with an October 1971 deadline.
tldr.outcome: The event brought together researchers and professionals working on network design, analysis and software.

today: RFC 157 is a historical record of an important early conference in computer networking. The symposium did take place and helped establish networking research as a recognized field.

sections.title: The Symposium Invitation
sections.content:
RFC 157 is a call for papers to the Second Symposium on Problems in the Optimization of Data Communication Systems, sponsored by ACM's SIGCOMM and the IEEE Computer Society. Vint Cerf at UCLA urged the early network researchers (the Network Working Group) to submit their work for presentation.

The symposium was to be held at Stanford University on October 20-22, 1971. Cerf noted that many NWG/RFC documents were already mature enough for publication, and encouraged participants not to hesitate submitting their protocol work and file transfer procedures for peer review.
sections.plainLanguage: The teacher of a group working on networks said 'Let's have a meeting in October where everyone shows their best work.' People were invited to write up their ideas about protocols and file transfer.

sections.title: Scope and Areas
sections.content:
The symposium called for papers in six broad areas: advances in data communication networks, computer communication technology, new applications and application models, software organization for communications, systems modeling and optimization, and interface problems and standards.

Papers were limited to 5,000 words and had to include an abstract. Submissions were due June 15, 1971, with final copy due August 21, 1971. Notification of acceptance was promised by July 21, 1971.
sections.plainLanguage: The meeting wanted papers about six topics: how to move data between computers, what technology to use, new ways to use networks, how to write network software, how to measure and improve networks, and how to make things fit together.

sections.title: Who Was Involved
sections.content:
The symposium was organized by SIGCOMM (the ACM's Special Interest Group on Communication) and the IEEE Computer Society's Technical Committee on Computer Communications. Vint Cerf of UCLA served as a point of contact, with general information available from P. E. Jackson at Bell Telephone Laboratories in New Jersey.

The event reflected the growing need to gather the distributed early network research community (which communicated primarily through RFCs distributed on paper) for direct discussion and exchange of ideas.
sections.plainLanguage: Computer groups from ACM and IEEE set up the meeting. Vint Cerf helped organize it. People from all over could submit ideas and come talk in person.
